claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature BCC phase after homogenization at approximately 1200°C.
Slow cooling followed by isothermal holding permits sufficient atomic diffusion for chemical ordering.
Slow cooling and isothermal holding produce ordered precipitates, such as B2, within the BCC matrix.
Rapid quenching suppresses atomic mobility and thereby prevents chemical ordering.
The controlled comparison uses identical samples from the same homogenized batch.
The baseline treatment is rapid quenching, while the comparison treatment is cooling at approximately 0.1°C/s followed by holding at 700°C for 1–10 hours.
The rapidly quenched baseline retains the metastable high-temperature BCC structure with minimal diffusion-driven ordering.
Differential diffusivities among Cr, Co, Fe, Ni, and Al generate local compositional fluctuations during slow cooling and isothermal holding.
Al, and possibly Cr, diffuse more slowly than Co, Fe, and Ni under the proposed thermal conditions.
The proposed diffusivity differences cause local elemental enrichment.
Local enrichment lowers the local free energy and triggers an order–disorder transition and nucleation of ordered precipitates.
Insufficient time for diffusion during rapid quenching preserves the metastable high-temperature BCC structure.
Relative to the quenched baseline, slow-cooled and held samples will develop additional superlattice reflections in XRD.
Relative to the quenched baseline, slow-cooled and held samples will exhibit local compositional modulations detectable by TEM and APT.
In-situ diffraction during cooling will capture early ordering events.
The mechanism should operate during slow cooling and intermediate-temperature holding but not during rapid quenching.
Significant residual stress or pre-existing compositional inhomogeneity could dominate the observed phase behavior and invalidate application of the proposed mechanism.
In-situ measurements can help distinguish differential-diffusivity effects from residual-stress and pre-existing-gradient effects.

Failure to observe any additional superlattice reflections, compositional modulation, or ordered phase in the slow-cooled and held samples relative to the quenched baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
